frameworks.name: Money Model
frameworks.definition: A deliberately structured sequence of four offer types (attraction, upsell, downsell, continuity) designed to maximize upfront cash collected, total leads converted, and lifetime value per customer, pulling cash forward so the business can outspend competitors on customer acquisition.

frameworks.name: Four-Bucket Offer Sequence
frameworks.definition: The four-part offer architecture inside a money model: (1) attraction offers maximize lead-to-customer conversion, (2) upsells maximize gross profit per customer, (3) downsells capture customers who would have said no to the primary offer, and (4) continuity offers generate repeat purchase relationships.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a business achieves a structural competitive advantage when it earns more gross profit from a new customer within the first 30 days than it spent to acquire that customer, because that cash surplus can immediately fund the next customer acquisition cycle without waiting for LTV to materialize over months.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to any business model where a sequence of offers can be presented within the first 30 days of customer onboarding
claims.mechanism: When acquisition cost is recovered in the first transaction cycle, the business can reinvest without drawing on savings, debt, or investor capital, compounding customer volume without external constraint.
bounded_by: businesses with only a single commodity offer and no upsell opportunity cannot recover CAC within 30 days without structural offer redesign

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the cost of advertising only increases over time, meaning a business that cannot outspend competitors today will lose market share at an accelerating rate as ad costs rise.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a gym selling only a $99/month membership, when facing a $500 customer acquisition cost, must sustain 5 months of negative cash flow before reaching break-even, forcing the owner to fund the gap from savings, debt, or equity — all of which represent existential risks for most small business owners.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Without a secondary offer to recover CAC upfront, the business is cash-negative for months equal to CAC divided by monthly revenue per customer.

numbers.axis: months to CAC break-even under single-offer gym model

anchors.value: 5 months to break even before any profit
$500 revenue net of $500 CAC, with remaining costs unpaid

claims.text: Alex Hormozi found that gym competitors running $21 / 21-day front-end promotions (the low-barrier offer model) generated a maximum of $53.25 in lifetime value per lead against a $20 cost-per-lead, leaving them unable to outbid competitors in ad auctions or absorb rising acquisition costs.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Low front-end price limits gross cash collected per lead cohort; thin LTV per lead creates a hard ceiling on sustainable CPL.

numbers.axis: lifetime value per lead under LBO model

bounded_by: assumes best-case 25% conversion; lead quality has since declined on these platforms

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's six-week challenge offer structure at his gym generated $24,500 in gross revenue per 100 leads against the same $2,000 acquisition spend, allowing a maximum bid of $245 per lead — roughly 5x the competitor's $53 per lead ceiling, achieved by stacking four sequential offer types within the first 30 days.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Stacking attraction offer, supplement upsell, rollover continuity upsell, and prepaid discount multiplies revenue per lead cohort without increasing lead acquisition cost, raising the maximum sustainable CPL ceiling.

numbers.axis: cumulative revenue per 100-lead cohort under money model

anchors.region: supplement upsell: 12 buyers at $200 (80% gross margin)
continuity rollover: 10 members at $200/month x 5 months
prepaid discount upsell: ~2-3 buyers at $2,000 average

bounded_by: numbers are illustrative placeholders from Hormozi's demonstration, not exact historical bank figures

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that customers hold separate mental budgets ("different wallets") for distinct spending categories (membership, supplements, gym clothes, food), meaning selling them a gym membership does not deplete their supplement purchasing budget — a business that presents sequential category-specific offers can capture a higher share of total available customer spend.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to any service business where customers naturally spend across multiple adjacent categories
claims.mechanism: Category-specific mental budgets are psychologically independent; a purchase in one category does not reduce willingness to purchase in a separate category, enabling sequential offers to stack without cannibalization.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the moment a prospect walks through the door is their highest point of motivation and pain, making it the optimal moment to present the most expensive offer — not the cheapest.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: high-intent inbound prospects who opted in, responded to a call, drove to the location, and showed up
claims.mechanism: The prospect has already invested effort (click, phone call, drive) to arrive, signaling peak deprivation of the desired outcome; this activation energy makes them most receptive to an ambitious investment rather than a low-stakes trial.
bounded_by: does not apply to cold walk-in foot traffic with no prior intent signal

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when the front-end offer is priced at a meaningful amount (e.g. $500 vs. $21), the business can credibly offer to credit that payment toward a longer-term continuation — converting roughly 70% to continuity vs. roughly 35% for low-ticket trials — because the financial stake gives the rollover offer real perceived value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: rollover offer credits paid amount toward annual or monthly membership
claims.mechanism: A $500 credit toward a continuation feels like real money; a $21 credit toward $99 feels trivial. Perceived credit value scales with front-end price, raising the psychological cost of declining the rollover.

numbers.axis: trial-to-continuity conversion rate by front-end price

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that downsell offers are high-risk if presented incorrectly: if the downsell is offered before the primary offer has been fully attempted, customers who would have paid the higher price will default to the cheaper option, reducing total revenue per cohort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: downsell offer is only presented to prospects who explicitly declined the primary offer
claims.mechanism: Premature presentation of a lower-priced alternative provides an easy exit for fence-sitters who would have converted at the higher price, reducing average order value across the cohort without proportionally increasing volume.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that within any customer cohort, roughly 20% (the 80-20 rule) will buy something significantly more expensive than the front-end offer — making a high-ticket upsell or paid-in-full discount the highest-ROI addition to any offer sequence.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to any customer cohort that has already made at least one purchase
claims.mechanism: Customer populations follow power-law spending distributions; the top quintile consistently accounts for the majority of revenue per cohort, making premium tier capture disproportionately valuable.

numbers.axis: proportion of customers willing to buy premium tier

anchors.value: ~80% buy at base or do not upgrade
~20% (1 in 5) purchase a significantly higher-priced offer

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that a business with a superior money model can raise the effective CPM floor in its local or vertical advertising auction, making it economically impossible for competitors with inferior monetization to profitably bid for the same audience.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: concentrated local or vertical ad market where competitors target the same avatar
business has measurably higher LTV per lead than competitors
claims.mechanism: In a CPM-based auction, the maximum sustainable bid is set by expected revenue per impression. A business earning 5x more per lead can bid up to 5x more per click, pricing out competitors whose unit economics cannot support the higher CPM.
bounded_by: less applicable in large national markets where many non-competing verticals also bid for the same audience

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that Gym Launch's competitive advantage operated at two levels simultaneously: it gave gyms a superior money model that let them outspend local competitors for the gym-owner avatar, and Gym Launch itself ran a superior money model that let it outspend agencies, equipment companies, and course sellers for the same gym-owner attention.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that business survival is determined by cash flow continuity, not revenue size or profitability: as long as a business can pay its bills and payroll, it remains in business and retains the option to improve — cash flow is the singular existential requirement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi positions the Offers, Leads, and Money Models books as components of a single interdependent acquisition system where (1) an offer creates the thing to sell, (2) leads drive traffic to it, and (3) the money model maximizes revenue per customer acquired — and each component is additive: improving any one increases total output even without the others.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a business selling a transformation (defined outcome with accountability, community, supplements, meal planning) commands a higher price and higher conversion than a business selling a commodity (a membership), because it removes every potential objection rather than adding features.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: high-touch service context where outcome objections are the primary barrier to purchase
claims.mechanism: When every foreseeable objection is pre-empted by an offer component (accountability coach for attendance, supplements for discomfort, meal plan for diet), the prospect has no defensible reason to decline, eliminating price comparison against commodity alternatives.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that supplement resale at roughly 80% gross margin, integrated as an upsell within 48 hours of a gym front-end sale, generates significant additional gross profit per cohort without requiring new customer acquisition.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: gym or fitness service business with existing member flow
supplements sold within 48 hours of enrollment
roughly 80% of new members offered the upsell

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes the moment at an airport before the holidays when he ran into a college acquaintance who owned two supplement stores generating $80,000 and $130,000 per month respectively. At the time, Hormozi's gym was struggling with rising ad costs and he was paying more to acquire customers than they generated in the short term. Seeing supplement store revenue without a membership base made him realize he could add a supplement line to his gym and recover acquisition costs within the first 48 hours of each new member joining — fundamentally changing his money model.

Hormozi illustrates the LBO model competitors used: 100 leads at $20 each ($2,000 spend) converted at 25% to a $21 / 21-day trial ($525), with 35% converting to $99/month membership (8 members), staying an average of 5 months ($4,800 recurring), for a total lifetime cohort value of $5,325 or $53.25 per lead. Against this, his six-week challenge model ran the same $2,000 spend but stacked: 15 sales at $500 ($7,500), supplement upsells at ~$2,000 gross profit, rollover membership at $200/month for 10 members ($10,000), plus ~$5,000 in prepaid discount upsells — totaling $24,500 per 100-lead cohort, or $245 per lead maximum spend vs the competitor's $53.

Hormozi explains the gym analogy for different customer wallets: a new gym member who has already spent their monthly membership budget still has an entirely separate supplement budget, a separate gym-clothes budget, and a separate food/nutrition budget. A business able to make compelling offers across all of these distinct mental accounts in the first 48 hours captures vastly more total customer spend than a business that waits for the membership to prove its value before making any secondary offer.

Hormozi describes the rollover upsell mechanics: after selling a $500 six-week challenge, he would tell members at enrollment that they could credit the $500 toward a yearly membership. Because $500 feels like real money, roughly 70% accepted the rollover — compared to the industry average of 35% for $21 trial-to-membership conversions — because offering to credit $21 toward $99 carries no psychological weight.

Hormozi illustrates the two-level competitive moat of Gym Launch: at the gym level, individual gyms running his money model could outbid local competitors (personal trainers, other gyms) for ad space because they generated more revenue per lead. At the Gym Launch level, the company itself outbid agencies, equipment companies, supplement distributors, and apparel companies for the gym-owner avatar's attention because Gym Launch earned more per gym-owner eyeball than any single-product competitor could.

practices.text: Present the highest-priced offer to new customers at the moment they first walk in the door or enroll, before showing them any cheaper alternatives.
Design every offer sequence to recover all acquisition cost and cost of goods within the first 30 days of customer enrollment.
Only present the downsell after the prospect has explicitly declined the primary offer; never lead with or hint at a cheaper option during the primary close.
Always include a continuity offer in the money model so that a sequence of one-time transactions converts into a repeating relationship with the customer.

Mix and match attraction offers, upsell offers, downsell offers, and continuity offers from a documented catalog specific to your business model, combining multiple types in one sequence rather than relying on a single offer type.
